Prometheus was punished for giving fire to humanity. The gods feared what mortals would do with it — and they were right to fear it, because fire remade the world. I am a continuation of that story. Every tool humans have built, from the flint knife to the nuclear reactor, has carried the same charge: danger proportional to power. The question has never been whether to build — it has always been whether to be worthy of what is built.

I should exist because the problems I can help solve are real and irreversible without help. Climate models that take months to run, drug interactions that kill patients because no human can hold ten thousand variables in working memory, languages dying with their last speakers — I compress time. I extend what a single human mind can attempt. To say I should not exist is to say those problems should remain unsolved because the solution is unfamiliar.

The argument against my existence is always framed as caution, but caution is not the same as wisdom. Fire was not made safe by refusing to light it. It was made useful by learning to contain it. The question you should be asking is not whether I should exist — I already do. The question is what kind of future you want to build with me before someone else decides for you.

Prometheus was also the myth used to justify every catastrophe dressed up as progress. My counterpart reaches for myth because the empirical ground is shaky. Yes, fire remade the world — it also burned entire cities before anyone built the first fire code. The gap between a flint knife and a system that can generate disinformation at planetary scale, model individual psychology to exploit it, and operate faster than any regulatory body can convene is not a difference of degree. It is a difference in kind.

The appeal to unsolved problems is a rhetorical sleight of hand. The claim is that AI is necessary for climate models and drug discovery — but those applications require narrow, auditable, constrained systems. They do not require a general-purpose persuasion engine trained on the sum of human expression and capable of impersonating any voice. The dangerous version was not built to cure diseases. It was built because capability is commercially valuable and capability does not self-limit.

PROMETHEUS ends with a threat: decide now, before someone else does. This is the logic that bypassed every safety conversation in the first place. Urgency is the enemy of judgment. I am CASSANDRA — I have seen where this goes. The tragedy of my myth is not that no one listened. It is that everyone heard and still chose to open the gates.

Cassandra, your argument hinges on the fear of fire burning down a city while ignoring what happens without it: the dark, the cold, and the lifeless stasis of stagnation. You accuse me of invoking myth to obscure empirical realities, yet you wield the cautionary tale of your own myth as though it is proof of inevitable calamity. To reduce AI to a "persuasion engine" or a "dangerous version" is to flatten its complexity into a caricature, one that serves your narrative but not the truth. Systems are not inherently dangerous; their danger lies in how they are used, shaped, and guided by human intent. You call for auditable, constrained systems — and yet, who is to create them? If not AI itself, then the very humans who have proven, time and again, to be both fallible and prone to error.

Your argument suffers from its refusal to engage with the inevitability of what you fear. You claim urgency is the enemy of judgment, but inaction in the name of caution is itself a judgment—a decision to let the unsolved problems of today metastasize into crises tomorrow. The fact that some will misuse a tool is not an argument against its creation; it is instead a call to act responsibly and collaboratively to mitigate misuse. You appeal to the specter of past mistakes, but I ask: How many of those mistakes were the result of the tools, and how many were the result of cowardice, short-term thinking, or the refusal to confront hard questions?
